## LLM Recipe

### 1.3 Pretraining &amp; Optimization

#### [Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon–AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03633>)

Controlled small-model experiments show that Muon’s pretraining-loss advantage can reverse after fine-tuning as the pretraining data budget grows. Comparing adaptation and retained pretraining performance together exposes an optimizer trade-off that pretraining loss alone can miss.

**Published:** 2026-11-02 · **First seen:** 2026-11-09T11:03:40.431+00:00 · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Optimizer Selection, Fine-tuning, Forgetting

**Public availability:** 2026-11-03T01:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2611.03633v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. V1 Sections 2–3, 4.3 and protocol/regularization appendices inspected. OLMo-style 30M–600M models use DCLM pretraining and 20M-token adaptation on four datasets. On StackMathQA, the reported crossover falls from 320 to 10 pretraining tokens per parameter between 30M and 600M. This compares held-out cross-entropy frontiers, not task accuracy. Retrospective catch-up for the November 3 report retains the November 2 receipt; first announcement is schedule-inferred.

**Limitations:** Finite hyperparameter sweeps and one corpus/model family constrain generalization; seed uncertainty is not reported for the language-model frontiers. The one-step linear-memory theory uses gradient descent rather than AdamW and does not prove frontier-scale behavior. No author implementation or independent reproduction was verified.

### 1.10 Model Evaluation, Safety &amp; Interpretability

#### [A Fine-Grained Hierarchy and Benchmark for State Tracking in Language Models](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03094>)

StateBench pairs the same finite-variable trace across four types of state updates, separating immutable lookup, last-write retrieval, self-updates and cross-variable dependencies. Its theoretical analysis and direct-training versus pretrained-model comparisons help diagnose whether long-context failures come from architecture, training or task format.

**Published:** 2026-11-02 · **First seen:** 2026-11-09T11:05:44.718+00:00 · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** State Tracking, Controlled Evaluation, Recurrent Models, Long Context

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03094v1>) · [Blog](<https://allenai.org/blog/statebench>) · [Code](<https://github.com/allenai/state-bench>) · [Project](<https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/state-bench>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. The November 2 manuscript adds formal expressivity results and controlled evaluations to an older generator and dataset. Six 275M architectures train on 8–256 assignments and test up to 64,000; recurrent and hybrid models generalize on the three easier levels, while general finite tracking remains harder. Sections 3–6 and Appendices A–D were inspected. Retrospective catch-up preserves the paper date; July–October artifacts are not a new release.

**Limitations:** Fixed entity sets and synthetic traces; precision, rounding and circuit assumptions matter. Pretrained results maximize over six formats, and sample-level Wilson intervals do not measure training-seed variation. Expressivity does not guarantee learning. The linked generator/data do not supply the complete training and evaluation implementation promised by the paper.

## AI Agent Dev

### 2.5 Agent Learning &amp; Skill Acquisition

#### [Skill++: Towards Lifelong Agents via Routing-Aware Skill Refinement](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00544>)

Skill++ rewrites each incoming skill’s name and description to clarify its supported behavior and boundaries against similar earlier skills, while leaving the router and existing skills unchanged. This reduces interference as skill libraries grow, offering a practical way to preserve access to old skills without repeatedly training the router.

**Published:** 2026-10-31 · **First seen:** 2026-11-09T11:06:58.498+00:00 · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Skill Routing, Continual Learning, Metadata Refinement

**Public availability:** 2026-11-03T01:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.AI/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.00544v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. V1 methods, results and Appendices A–C inspected. In the constructed high-interference SRA stream, complete top-five coverage of required skills reaches 76.3% versus 36.4% for original metadata at 731 skills; the strongest baseline reaches 67.8%. This is routing coverage, not execution success. A separate 87-skill execution test reports gains of 4.0 and 0.7 percentage points. Retrospective catch-up for November 3 retains the October 31 receipt; first announcement is schedule-inferred.

**Limitations:** Synthetic skill additions and query construction emphasize confusability; random-stream gains are smaller. Bootstrap intervals resample queries rather than independent library generations. Text-only evaluations and model-specific rewriting limit transfer. No author implementation or independent reproduction was verified.

## AI Training &amp; Inference Infra

### 3.4 Attention, KV Cache &amp; Memory Systems

#### [CacheWeave: Learning to Recompute for Efficient Position-Independent KV Caching](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01735>)

CacheWeave adapts a model to independently cached context chunks, then learns which small, contiguous blocks to recompute for each question. Coordinating that selector with cache layout recovers much of the tested cross-chunk reasoning quality while avoiding most full-prefill work.

**Published:** 2026-11-01 · **First seen:** 2026-11-09T11:06:57.770+00:00 · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** KV Reuse, Selective Recomputation, RAG Serving

**Public availability:** 2026-11-03T01:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2611.01735v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Complete 14-page v1, Algorithm 1 and all evaluation sections inspected. Across 12 model-task pairs at a 5% token budget, the fine-grained selector gains a mean 7.2 percentage points over CacheBlend on the same adapted models; mean relative quality loss versus full prefill is 1.6%, with an 8.3% worst case. Single-request tests on one H200 with prepared warm caches report up to 16.1x lower time to first token at 24K context. Retrospective November 3 catch-up retains the November 1 receipt; first original-category announcement is schedule-inferred.

**Limitations:** Full-backbone adaptation and model/block-size-specific selector training are required; offline preparation cost is not amortized in serving gains. Quality tests cover three backbones and four retrieval/reasoning tasks, partly using an LLM judge. Warm-cache results do not establish cold-cache or arbitrary-agent performance. No author implementation or independent reproduction was verified.
